title: China SIM Card & Internet
intro: Getting online in China is the single most important pre-trip task — Google, Instagram and many apps are blocked on local networks. Your options: an international eSIM (easiest), a Chinese physical SIM (local number), or roaming.
body: International eSIM (recommended for short trips)

Buy online before you fly from providers such as Airalo, Holafly, Nomad or Holafly. Plans run roughly $12–18 for 10–15 GB over 15 days. Because data routes via Hong Kong or Singapore servers, Google, WhatsApp and Instagram work without a VPN. Install and activate the eSIM QR code at home — some codes fail to load once inside the firewall. Your phone keeps its home number for calls.
Chinese physical SIM (best for stays 1 month+)

At airport counters or city stores of China Unicom (green), China Mobile (red) or China Telecom: bring your passport — a face scan and registration are required. You get a local number (useful for Didi rides and food delivery apps) plus data for ~¥40–100/month. Popular tourist packages: 10 GB/15 days around ¥85–130. Carry the passport with you when buying.
Wi-Fi & hotspot
Free Wi-Fi is common in hotels, malls, airports and metros (often needs a local number for SMS verification). A pocket Wi-Fi rental (~¥30/day) is a solid backup for groups.
VPN note
If you rely on your home carrier's roaming instead of an eSIM, install a VPN before arrival. Google Play / Apple App Store downloads of VPN apps may be restricted inside China — do it at home.
tips: Install & test your eSIM before boarding. Keep your original SIM for SMS. Download offline maps (maps.me, Baidu Maps EN) and a translation app before you land.

title: Visa & Entry
intro: Most travelers now enter China visa-free or visa-free-in-transit. Two policies matter most in 2026: the 240-hour transit policy and bilateral visa exemptions.
body: 240-hour visa-free transit (10 days)

Citizens of 55+ countries (US, UK, most of Europe, Australia, Japan, South Korea, Indonesia and more) can transit China visa-free for up to 240 hours / 10 days — provided they hold an onward ticket (confirmed date & seat) to a third country or region. Entry is via 60 designated ports across 24 provinces; you may travel within the permitted region for tourism and business. This is ideal for layover trips (e.g. US→Beijing 5 days→Japan).
Bilateral visa-free entry

China has mutual visa-exemption agreements with several countries (e.g. Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, UAE, Qatar, Belarus and others, for 15–30 days) — check with your local Chinese embassy or visa service before relying on it.
Standard tourist (L) visa

For longer stays or trips that don't fit transit rules: apply at a China Visa Application Service Center with passport (6+ months validity), photos, itinerary and hotel bookings. Processing is usually 4–7 working days; costs vary by country and entry type.
On arrival & registration
Bring your passport everywhere — hotels and some attractions require it. Police registration is handled by hotels for foreign guests automatically.
tips: Always keep a printed copy of your onward ticket for transit entry. Enter through the ports that match your permitted region. Double-check policy updates before departure — rules change frequently.

title: Currency & Payments
intro: China is nearly cashless, but foreign cards now work easily. Set up Alipay and WeChat Pay before you fly and you'll pay like a local.
body: Alipay (international version)

Download the Alipay app, register with your home phone number (choose your country code), then add a Visa, Mastercard, JCB, Diners Club or Discover card under 'Add Now'. No Chinese bank account needed. Pay by scanning QR codes everywhere — taxis, hotels, street food, trains.
WeChat Pay

Same flow inside WeChat: Me → Pay and Services → Wallet → Bank Cards → Add a Bank Card. Visa, Mastercard, American Express, JCB, Diners Club and Discover are accepted. Complete the setup at home — brand-new accounts may face a security check, easier to sort out before arrival.
Cash & cards
¥100–500 cash is a sensible backup (rural areas and small vendors). International ATMs accept Visa/Mastercard/UnionPay. Hotel card terminals accept foreign cards; some small shops are cash/QR only.
Wallet apps & UnionPay
Alipay+ also lets travelers pay with their home e-wallets in some cases. UnionPay cards work broadly. Keep both Alipay and WeChat installed — a few merchants only take one.
tips: Set a payment limit and enable fingerprint/face pay. Carry your passport when adding cards for identity verification. Prices are in CNY — the apps convert charges transparently.

title: Transportation
intro: China's high-speed rail is the best way to travel between cities — and booking it as a foreigner is easier than ever.
body: High-speed rail (高铁)

350 km/h trains link every major city: Beijing→Shanghai 4.5h, Beijing→Xi'an 4.5h, Chengdu→Leshan 1h, Shanghai→Suzhou 25 min. Book with your passport number on Trip.com or the official 12306 app; collect tickets at the station with your passport, or use e-ticket + passport scan. Fares: 2nd class ¥553 (Beijing–Shanghai); business class ~4× that.
Flights
Domestic flights are cheap and frequent (Beijing–Chengdu from ¥600). Note: use full passport names matching the booking. Check in online or at counter — domestic security is strict.
Metro & city travel

Beijing, Shanghai, Chengdu, Xi'an, Hangzhou and 40+ cities have metros. Use the Alipay/WeChat transit QR codes, or buy single tickets at machines (many accept foreign cards). Taxis: use Didi (English version) — pay via Alipay/WeChat linked card. Never hail unlicensed cabs.
Practical times
Taxis from airport: Beijing ~¥150–250, Shanghai ~¥200. Metro from airport ~¥7–10. Book long-distance trains 15 days ahead in peak seasons (Spring Festival, Oct Golden Week, summer).
tips: Download Trip.com or 12306 + Didi before arrival. Print or screenshot hotel addresses in Chinese characters for taxi drivers. Avoid traveling on the last 3 days before Chinese New Year.

title: Useful Travel Tips
intro: A few things that make China travel smooth, safe and comfortable.
body: Language
English is limited outside tourist hubs. Use translation apps (Google Translate offline packs, or Microsoft Translator) and carry written Chinese for addresses. Menu scanning apps help with food.
Weather & packing

China spans all climates: Beijing dry & cold winters, hot summers; Shanghai humid; Harbin −25°C in Jan; Sanya tropical year-round. Pack layers, comfortable walking shoes, and a power adapter (220V, sockets Type A/C/I).
Health & water
Drink bottled or boiled water. Pharmacies (药店) are everywhere; international-standard hospitals exist in Beijing, Shanghai, Chengdu. Travel insurance covering medical care is strongly recommended.
Safety & etiquette

China is extremely safe for tourists. No tipping is expected — round up occasionally. In temples & museums: no flash photography of artifacts, dress modestly. Queues are taken seriously; line up at stations and attractions.
Internet
Remember the connectivity guide: eSIM installed before arrival, or a VPN ready if using home roaming. Alipay/WeChat QR codes also unlock free Wi-Fi in many public places.
tips: Save a screenshot of your hotel name in Chinese + a map pin. Keep a photo of your passport page and visa in your phone. Learn two phrases: 谢谢 (thanks) and 多少钱? (how much?).

title: Health, Insurance & Hospitals
intro: China's public hospitals are affordable and, in tier-1 cities, modern — but you must pay a deposit first and claim back from travel insurance later. This guide covers what to pack, how to see a doctor, and why insurance is non-negotiable.
body: Travel insurance — buy before you fly

Comprehensive travel medical cover is essential: a broken leg or appendicitis abroad can cost ¥30,000–100,000+ without insurance. Buy a policy that covers China explicitly (most global plans do) and includes emergency evacuation, since remote areas such as Tibet or Xinjiang have limited trauma care. Keep the insurer's 24/7 hotline and policy number saved offline. Compare on price and China-specific cover rather than brand.
If you get sick: the 5-step route

1) Call your insurer's assistance line first — they arrange hospitals and guarantees. 2) Ask your hotel to recommend a 三甲 (Grade-A) hospital; in major cities English-speaking international clinics exist (Beijing United Family, Shanghai Pudong International Medical). 3) Bring your passport — clinics register foreign patients with it. 4) Pay the deposit (usually ¥200–2,000 for outpatient) and keep every receipt and medical record for your claim. 5) Submit the claim after you return; translate receipts if requested.
Pharmacies & common medicines

Chain pharmacies stock cold medicine, painkillers, antiseptics and diarrhea remedies over the counter without a prescription. Antibiotics require a doctor's prescription. Bring your own regular prescription medicines with a doctor's letter, plus basics: rehydration salts, sunscreen, motion-sickness tablets, and a small first-aid kit. Medicine names come in Chinese only — show the pharmacist the ingredient name (e.g. paracetamol = 对乙酰氨基酚).
Emergencies & numbers to save

In emergencies dial 120 (ambulance); 110 (police) and 119 (fire). The all-in-one government hotline 12345 can connect you to translation help in major cities. On heavy-pollution days reduce outdoor time. For altitude sickness, acclimatize 1–2 days before trekking above 3,500 m in Tibet/Yunnan/Qinghai and consider medication prescribed before departure.
tips: Save your insurer hotline and policy number offline before departure. Note the address of the nearest international hospital in your first city.

title: Accessible Travel in China
intro: China is improving accessibility fast but unevenly: modern metros, airports and new stations are wheelchair-friendly, while old town lanes and temple steps remain hard. Plan route by route — this guide tells you what works and how to ask for help.
body: Where accessibility is good

High-speed rail (CRH) has wide doors, accessible toilets and boarding assistance if you call 12306 ahead; airports provide free wheelchair service on request. Subway lines built after 2010 in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen have elevators and level boarding. New museums and scenic-area visitor centers (e.g. Forbidden City, Summer Palace, Zhangjiajie) offer ramps and wheelchairs to borrow — book the loan when you buy your ticket.
Where you need a plan B

Classic old-town districts (Lijiang, Pingyao, Wuzhen, Hongcun) and most mountain/temple sites involve cobblestones, stairs or cable-car gaps. For mountains, the cable car plus a short walk is usually the accessible option (Huangshan, Emei, Huashan). Carry a printed note in Chinese: 我需要无障碍通道/轮椅服务 (I need accessible access / wheelchair service).
Taxis, hotels & practical help

Standard taxis rarely have ramps; book wheelchair-accessible cars via DiDi (the accessibility option) or hotel concierge. Choose hotels built after 2015 with elevators and grab bars — filter on Booking/Agoda by 'accessible bathroom'. Key public spaces meet accessible standards; small restaurants and rural B&Bs usually do not. If you need assistance in public venues, call 12345 and ask for the disability services window.
tips: Book wheelchair loans and accessible tickets before you travel — most big sites and airports require advance request.

title: Hotels & Where to Stay
intro: From 5-star international chains to ¥150 family guesthouses, China's hotel market covers every budget. The key decisions are location, star level vs. actual quality, and booking through platforms that speak your language.
body: Choosing the right area

For first-timers, stay inside the 2nd Ring Road in Beijing (Dongcheng/Xicheng), around People's Square in Shanghai, or within walking distance of the old town in Lijiang/Pingyao/Wuzhen — you pay a premium but save hours of transit. For mountain parks (Zhangjiajie, Huangshan, Emei), book a hotel at the scenic-area gate the night before an early-morning entry, or stay one night on the mountain for sunrise.
Star ratings: read the gap

Chinese star ratings (五星/四星) are set by local tourism bureaus and often lag real quality — a 2010 5-star can be worse than a 2021 4-star. Filter by year of renovation and read recent English reviews. International chains (Hilton, Marriott, IHG, Accor) guarantee consistent quality in tier-1 cities. Mid-range domestic brands (Ji Hotel, Atour, Lavande) offer clean, modern rooms at ¥250–450 in most cities.
Booking, check-in & practical notes

Book via Agoda/Booking for English support and free cancellation, or Ctrip (Trip.com) for the widest inventory including small-town guesthouses. All hotels register foreign guests with your passport — always carry it (a photocopy is not enough). Payment: international cards work at large chains; small hotels prefer Alipay/WeChat Pay, so set those up (see the Payments guide).
tips: Request a scenic-view room at booking time, not at check-in. Carry your passport for every hotel check-in.
